strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in pixel-based MBRL: the tendency of standard reconstruction objectives (e.g., MSE/L2) to prioritize large visual background elements while dropping small, task-critical objects.

Well-motivated integration of modern foundation video object segmentation (Cutie): leveraging Cutie's compact object memory vectors directly rather than coarse binary masks is computationally effective and avoids information loss from spatial downsampling.

Evaluation extends beyond standard benchmarks to Hollow Knight, a modern, visually complex, high-resolution action game. The authors developed a custom wrapper, modding hooks, and virtualized execution pipeline, demonstrating genuine practical utility in challenging visual domains.

Comprehensive experimental analysis and ablations, including vector vs. mask representations, qualitative reconstruction checks of object latents, sensitivity to few-shot label counts (1-shot vs. 6-shot), and robustness against tracking failures.
weaknesses: Requires manual human annotation (6 frames per Atari game, 12 per Hollow Knight boss) and an environment-specific, predetermined number of objects $K$. While practical, this departs from the standard self-supervised / autonomous paradigm of visual MBRL benchmarks.

On the Atari 100k benchmark, the performance gains are somewhat mixed: while the human-normalized mean improves from 114.2% to 134.8% over the local STORM* baseline, the median score increases only marginally (42.5% to 43.8%), and purely self-supervised methods like DIAMOND (146% mean) or DreamerV3 (49% median) achieve competitive results without requiring external annotations or foundation models.

Lack of wall-clock time and computational throughput analysis: Running Cutie's video segmentation model alongside the world model inevitably incurs memory and inference overhead, but the paper does not report FPS, training time, or hardware resource comparisons against baseline STORM.

Current formulation struggles with multiple identical/duplicate instances (e.g., Mantis Lords, MsPacman pellets) and assumes a fixed number of objects, limiting its immediate plug-and-play generality in open-ended scenes.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-recognized limitation in pixel-based world models (MBRL): the tendency of reconstruction losses (e.g., L2/Huber) to wash out small, dynamic, decision-critical entities against complex visual backgrounds.

Well-motivated integration of a frozen foundation video object segmentation model (Cutie), demonstrating that utilizing internal compact object memory vectors (rather than downsampled binary masks) is computationally efficient and retains fine-grained object state and localization details.

Compelling evaluation on a novel and visually rich testbed (Hollow Knight boss fights), demonstrating practical applicability to complex commercial games with distracting visual effects where standard world models typically fail to reconstruct characters accurately.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and ablations, including comparisons between vector and mask representations, sensitivity to the number of annotation frames (1-shot vs 6-shot), actor-critic architectures (MLP vs spatial attention), and robustness against segmentation failure/dropout.
weaknesses: Requires manual human annotation (6 frames per Atari game, 12 per Hollow Knight boss) and manual specification of the number of objects $K$. This human-in-the-loop requirement contrasts with standard autonomous reinforcement learning pipelines and limits scalability across large task suites.

Performance improvements on the standardized Atari 100k benchmark are relatively modest in aggregate: while HNS mean increases from 114.2% to 134.8% over the baseline STORM*, the median HNS shows negligible improvement (42.5% to 43.8%), and purely self-supervised baselines like DIAMOND still achieve higher overall mean scores without requiring object annotations.

Difficulty handling identical or duplicate instances (e.g., pellets in Ms. Pac-Man or multiple identical enemies), which is an inherent limitation of the chosen single-object tracking/segmentation paradigm.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental failure mode in pixel-based MBRL: standard $L_2$ reconstruction losses often fail to capture small, task-critical objects in visually rich environments.

Demonstrates an ambitious empirical application on the visually complex game Hollow Knight, providing a novel platform and detailed system integration (Windows VM, screenshot capture, modding API) for evaluating MBRL beyond standard toy/Atari domains.
Provides informative ablation studies, specifically analyzing vector versus mask representations, policy architecture choices (MLP vs. attention), and robustness to tracking failure/zeroing.
weaknesses: Requires manual human annotation of segmentation masks (6 frames per Atari game, 12 per Hollow Knight boss) and manual predetermination of object count $K$. This introduces privileged human supervision that breaks the self-supervised, autonomous nature of model-based reinforcement learning and limits scalability to open-ended settings.

Despite having access to ground-truth object identity via human annotations and a powerful foundation model (Cutie), performance gains on Atari 100k are modest: median human-normalized score improves only marginally (from 42.5% to 43.8%), which is lower than DreamerV3 (49%), while unassisted approaches like DIAMOND achieve higher mean scores (146% vs. 134.8%) without manual annotation.

Algorithmic novelty is relatively limited, consisting primarily of an engineering pipeline combining an off-the-shelf video object segmentation model (Cutie) with an existing world model architecture (STORM) via standard spatial and temporal attention blocks.

The evaluation on Hollow Knight suffers from confounding factors; in addition to introducing object features, the authors altered the reward function and termination scheme (treating hit loss as virtual termination), making it difficult to isolate the precise source of performance gains relative to prior work.

The approach struggles significantly with duplicate identical entities (e.g., MsPacman, Mantis Lords) and non-discrete background structures (e.g., Gopher tunnels), which represents a known and major bottleneck for the proposed object-centric pipeline.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in pixel-based model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL): the tendency of pixel reconstruction losses to neglect small, task-critical objects in visually dynamic and cluttered environments.

Proposes an effective and pragmatic paradigm combining few-shot foundation video segmentation models (Cutie/SAM2) with transformer-based world models (STORM), avoiding the optimization hurdles and visual domain limitations of purely unsupervised slot-attention methods.

Demonstrates strong performance on visually rich environments, particularly Hollow Knight boss fights, where standard world models fail due to background complexity, as well as on Atari 100k and Meta-World continuous control tasks.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and ablations, including comparisons between vector-based and mask-based representations (demonstrating why compact vector features outperform FOCUS-style masks), sensitivity to segmentation failures, annotation quantity, and computational overhead measurements.
weaknesses: Relies on manual human annotation of key objects (6 to 12 frames per environment) and manual specification of the object count K, which reduces the complete autonomy of the RL agent compared to purely self-supervised or unsupervised approaches.

On the Atari 100k benchmark, while the mean Human-Normalized Score (HNS) increases substantially, the median HNS shows only a marginal gain (from 42.5% in STORM to 43.8% in OC-STORM), and lags behind some existing MBRL baselines (e.g., Δ-IRIS at 59.4% median, TWM at 50.5% median) that do not require external annotations.

The Hollow Knight benchmark lacks standardization across the literature; the custom reward shaping (e.g., treating being hit as a virtual episode termination) and action space mapping make it difficult to compare directly against broader external baselines beyond the authors' own STORM reimplementation.

strengths: Well-motivated approach: Effectively identifies and tackles a core vulnerability of reconstruction-based world models—namely, the tendency of pixel losses to prioritize visually dominant backgrounds over small, task-critical foreground objects.

Practical integration of vision foundation models: Demonstrates how few-shot video segmentation models (Cutie and SAM 2) can provide compact, semantically rich object representations with minimal human annotation effort (6–12 frames), bypassing the fragility of purely unsupervised slot-based discovery methods.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Validated across three diverse testbeds, including Atari 100k (26 games), challenging boss fights in the visually intricate modern game Hollow Knight, and continuous control in Meta-world.

Thorough ablations and practical insights: Compares vector-based vs. mask-based representations, examines sensitivity to segmentation dropouts/failures, evaluates annotation budget scaling, and provides realistic runtime and latency measurements on consumer/workstation GPUs.
weaknesses: Reliance on human supervision and prior knowledge: While annotating 6–12 frames is lightweight, it still introduces privileged domain knowledge (identifying and segmenting the exact critical objects) not available to purely self-supervised MBRL baselines (such as standard STORM, DreamerV3, or DIAMOND), making direct sample-efficiency comparisons somewhat unequal.

Fixed object capacity and handling of dynamic instances: The framework requires pre-specifying a fixed number of objects $K$, which struggles with dynamically appearing/disappearing objects, multiple identical instances (e.g., duplicated enemies as noted in Section 7), and amorphous environmental features (e.g., breakable walls or tunnels).

Moderate competitive advantage over state-of-the-art on Atari 100k: Despite incorporating object priors, OC-STORM achieves an HNS median of 43.8%, which trails several annotation-free world model baselines in Table 2 (such as $\Delta$-IRIS at 59.4% median and TWM at 50.5% median).

Incremental architectural novelty: The core modeling contributions largely combine known mechanisms—feeding extracted visual/object tokens into categorical VAEs and alternating spatial-temporal attention blocks—rather than proposing fundamentally new dynamics modeling principles.

strengths: Pragmatic approach to object-centric RL: Leveraging modern open-set video segmentation models (Cutie, SAM2) via few-shot prompting (6–12 frames) is a well-motivated and practical middle ground between brittle unsupervised slot-based object discovery and heavily supervised per-frame annotations.

Compelling evaluation on visually complex domains: Demonstrating effective model-based RL in *Hollow Knight* boss fights directly addresses the known failure mode of pixel-reconstruction MBRL (where small, task-critical foreground sprites are drowned out by complex, dynamic backgrounds).

Thorough empirical analysis and ablations: The paper provides insightful analyses comparing vector-based vs. mask-based representations, evaluating sensitivity to annotation counts (1-shot vs. 6-shot), testing robustness against tracking failures/dropouts, and detailing system latency/computational overhead.

Architectural flexibility: The hybrid spatial-temporal world model design supports both transformer (STORM) and recurrent (DreamerV3) backbones and seamlessly fuses object-level latents with raw visual latents.
weaknesses: Reliance on manual human supervision: Although the annotation requirement is few-shot, identifying which entities are task-relevant and manually annotating initial frames breaks the end-to-end, autonomous learning paradigm standard in Atari/pixel RL benchmarks.

Fixed entity count and struggles with duplicate instances: The framework relies on a fixed, predefined number of object slots $K$ per game, making it difficult to handle open-ended environments where objects dynamically appear, vanish, or duplicate (e.g., as noted with the multiple bosses in Mantis Lords or individual bricks in Breakout).

Incremental gains on Atari 100k: On the Atari 100k benchmark, the median Human-Normalized Score improvement over baseline STORM is modest (43.8% vs. 42.5%), showing that when background distractions are minimal, the additional complexity of the segmentation pipeline yields diminishing returns.

Pipeline complexity and inference overhead: Introducing heavy vision foundation models adds non-negligible engineering complexity, memory footprint, and inference latency during rollout collection and preprocessing.
